newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Horse Racing-Irish racing on slow road to recovery.
newsitem.headline: Horse Racing-Irish racing on slow road to recovery.

text.p: Horse racing, as much a part of Ireland's proud heritage as Guinness, is turning the corner to recovery after years of trailing the field of popular pastimes.
Beaten into a distant fourth place by television, soccer and a combination of the two, race track attendance has fallen and betting is down by almost 20 percent.
But in a year when the fast-growing Irish economy has been likened to a "Celtic Tiger" horse racing is seen on the slow road to recovery and a rescue plan is being drawn up.

1996 was a year of growth and development for the sport in Ireland with an eight percent rise in attendance levels, a 13 percent increase in on-course betting turnover and a six percent jump in prize money.

"They are not staggering increases but certainly they are very positive. They represent an improvement over recent years and hopefully we have now turned the corner," Noel Ryan, Chief Executive of the Irish Horseracing Authority, said.

The IHA, which has overall responsibility for the administration of racing in Ireland, said in its review of racing statistics for 1996 that 1.10 million people attended 258 racing fixtures at Ireland's 25 racecourses in 1996.
It said the aim was to increase annual attendances by 200,000 paying customers to 1.3 million by the year 2001 and that its main target area would be the younger generation.
The IHA said a total of 76.08 punts ($121.6) was bet with on-course bookmakers in 1996 while prize money for the year totalled 13.95 million Irish pounds.

Denis Brosnan, IHA Chairman, said the ultimate objective was to create a vibrant racing industry with racecourse facilities at Ireland's major racecourses on a par with the best elsewhere and with all tracks upgraded in standard.
"We need also to increase prize-money and sponsorship," Brosnan said. "To enable all these objectives to be achieved, we need to put the funding of the industry on a sound footing."
To this end, the IHA said it would radically transform the Tote, a cash and credit betting service on-course and an off- course credit betting service.

The IHA said in its strategic plan for the development of the Irish Thoroughbred Racing Industry 1997-2001 that it planned to transform the Tote so that it contributed substantially to the income of the Authority for reinvestment and reduce the cost-base in Irish racing.
"The Tote has the potential to bridge the gap between the finance currently available to the industry, which is adequate, and the level of finance that it so desperately needs," Brosnan said.
"We have set ourselves an ambitious target in relation to the Tote but we believe that it is realistic and attainable," he added.
The IHA said in the meantime, and pending the generation of additional income from within, it would be looking to the Irish government for increased support.
Tote betting increased by almost nine per cent to 19.53 million punts, of which 3.6 million punts was attributable to credit betting, in 1996.
With Tote retention averaging 21 per cent, the gross retention from the Tote in 1996 was estimated at 4.2 million punts.

But operating costs of 3.6 million punts were incurred in running the business with the result that the net contribution to racing from the operation of the Tote last year was estimated at 0.6 million punts.
The IHA said it was forecasting that the Tote will establish a High Street betting business with turnover of seven million punts by the year 2001.

In response, Stewart Kenny, spokesman for the Allied Betting Shops Association, said considerable research had been carried out into the viability of Tote betting products and Ireland's off-course punters were found to be uninterested in Irish racing.
The IHA said it was also forecasting a further growth in Tote credit betting from 3.6 million punts to seven million punts by the year 2001.
This will bring the total Tote turnover from its 1996 level of 19.5 million punts to 34.3 million punts in the year 2001, the IHA said.

The IHA said if the right steps were taken to reduce significantly the cost of operating the Tote, with a turnover of 34.3 million punts by the year 2001, an overall net contribution of 2.5 million punts would accrue to racing.
"The capital cost of bringing this about will be substantial both in terms of restructuring (staff-related costs) and investment in technology and equipment.
After the pay-back period, racing will have available a substantial new source of income to improve prize-money and develop the industry more fully," Brosnan said.
